## **Notes** 

###### Units used: 

Unless otherwise stated, all statistics on platinum and palladium supply and demand are expressed in terms of fine metal content.  All references in this publication to “ounces” refer to troy ounces. 

**One troy ounce =** 31.103 grammes **One tonne =** 32,151 troy ounces **“dollar”** US dollar unless otherwise stated 

###### Prices: 

Unless otherwise stated, US dollars and their equivalents are for the pm fixes of the London Platinum and Palladium Market. 

Terminology: 

Estimates of **supply** _include_ mine production and the recycling of both scrapped autocatalysts and old jewellery but _exclude_ contributions from above-ground stocks, such as supplies from stocks controlled by state institutions in Russia. 

**Demand** estimates are _net_ of recycling with the exception of autocatalyst and jewellery, where _gross_ demand is shown. i.e. the total amount of metal supplied to these two sectors.  Estimates of recycling from scrapped autocatalysts and jewellery are shown separately as part of supply given their scale and potential for change.  (This year’s survey is the second in which we have presented jewellery fabrication as gross with a separate series for scrap; prior to this, jewellery was shown on a net basis.)  Estimates of demand exclude the movements of any above-ground stocks held within the specified industries, for example any changes in stocks held by the automotive industry. 

By simple arithmetic, this leaves either a **“Gross Surplus or Deficit”** before any movements in above-ground stocks are considered.  This is a critical measure of the underlying fundamentals of platinum and palladium and indicates the extent to which fabrication demand may have depended on the release of above-ground stocks,

or otherwise.  At the same time, this also indicates the change in global above-ground stocks. 

Unless otherwise stated, all references to **“above-ground stocks”** of platinum and palladium refer to stocks of refined metal, of a form and quality accepted as good delivery in the Zurich market and the world’s principal commodity exchanges.  Our supply/demand tables also show **“Estimated Movements in Stocks”** .  These specific movements relate only to above-ground stock holdings for which reasonable estimates of movement can be made and attributed. A listing and breakdown of these appears in the more detailed tables in the Appendices section of this Survey. 

Having allowed for the Estimated Movements in Stocks as defined above, the **“Residual Surplus or Deficit”** is arrived at by deduction.  A **residual deficit** implies the extent to which **_other above-ground stocks_** , including those held by financial institutions and/or investors, were released to meet fabrication demand.  Conversely a **residual surplus** implies the extent to which these **_other above-ground stock_** holdings were added to.  However, this should not be construed as indicating the change in global above-ground stocks.  For this, please refer to the reported Gross Surplus or Deficit. 

**Throughout the tables, totals may not add due to independent rounding.**

### **1. Executive Summary** 

###### **Introduction & Prices** 

In terms of the macro investment drivers for precious metals (and gold in particular), little has changed since our previous forecast in March of this year.  Interest rates in the developed world are extraordinarily low by historical standards (negative in real terms), monetary policy remains exceptionally loose (especially in the United States), while elevated oil and food prices are stoking inflation.  Furthermore, with Greece teetering on the brink of default, sovereign debt is still a major headache within the European Union, while the burden of government debt in the US is increasingly worrying and has contributed to material dollar weakness this year.  (As we write, the Obama administration is battling Congress for a further increase in the nation’s debt-ceiling; without which the Fed is warning that the government may soon run out of money). 

Superimposed on this, the near-term prospects for economic growth appear fragile in both the US and in Europe, while the economy in disaster-struck Japan is likely to shrink this year.  Meanwhile, the Chinese government has been raising interest rates and increasing reserve requirements for its banks in a bid to dampen credit and cool inflation – measures which in turn risk a material slow-down in economic growth. 

Taken together, these factors continue to be especially favourable for gold (with the price hitting $1,500 for the 

first time ever in April) but convey mixed messages for platin

um and palladium; these being primarily industrial metals. While the overarching backdrop of minimal interest rates, lax monetary policy, rising inflation and a weak dollar are favourable conditions for platinum and palladium investment (opportunity costs being minimal, with cash non-returning and depreciating), the nearterm economic prospects are less enticing in terms of underlying fabrication demand. This most likely explains what has been a period of fairly subdued trading over recent months (relative to gold) with both metals having struggled to gather much by way of sustainable forward momentum. That said, the prices of both metals remain elevated (substantially ahead of last year’s robust averages), supported in the main by extensive investment positions in both exchange traded funds (ETFs) and futures, although exposure levels in futures have continued to be volatile. On the plus side for palladium, the continuation of an underlying gross deficit (this year and beyond) and the anticipated conclusion of Russian government sales have provided a degree of price tension. In the case of platinum, however, the same can hardly be said given that underlying gross surplus conditions are likely to persist for some time. However, the challenges of platinum mining in South Africa (fragile economics and Platinum Gross Surplus/Defcit Forecasts

When it comes to assessing likely price trajectories, this leaves us with the challenge of weighing-up both the likely behaviour of investors and the influence of the underlying fundamentals. In the case of the former, we remain of the view that the broader climate for precious metals investment will remain favourable over the rest of 2011 and throughout 2012. This is premised on the assumption of ample global liquidity and the reluctance among the developed economies to materially rein this in, or make significant upward adjustments in interest rates, before the prospects for sustainable economic growth are more assured. However, as we move into 2013, we expect those assurances to crystallise,

with the emergence of greater economic and financial stability enabling that process to begin. Inevitably, this will reflect less favourably on the investment case for precious metals, and with weakening sentiment, there is a likelihood of moderate outflows of investment funds over the latter part of that year. Looking at the underlying fundamentals, although easing somewhat, platinum is expected to register substantial gross surpluses over the forecast period, causing above-ground stocks to rise still further. This means that platinum is very heavily exposed to sentiment within the investment community, which will be asked to continue absorbing this excess platinum. For the reasons we have described already, we believe investors will be willing to do this for some time yet, and furthermore will be willing to do so at generally elevated prices (in nominal dollar terms) – despite platinum’s underlying gross surplus and increasing stocks. However, as we have said, investor sentiment is likely to turn less favourable by the time we reach 2013. We therefore forecast nominal average platinum prices of $1,813 in 2011, $1,779 in 2012 and finally, an average of $1,657 in 2013. Although weakening towards the end of the forecast period, this profile compares favourably (in nominal terms at least) with platinum’s average in 2010, which at $1,611 was an all-time high. Meanwhile, palladium is forecast to remain in gross deficit over the whole of the forecast period, resulting in the erosion of above-ground stocks (although these remain substantial). As a result, a degree of net disinvestment of palladium holdings will be required in order to balance the market. With Russian government sales forecast to decline materially from 2012, that means this disinvestment from that time will increasingly have to come from investor holdings. Inevitably, in our view, this will necessitate higher prices, despite the anticipated weakening of the broader investment climate we expect from 2013. Accordingly, we forecast nominal average prices for palladium of $793 in 2011, and an increase to $954 in 2012. Thereafter, allowing for some deterioration in investment drivers during 2013, we expect a more slender gain to an average for that year of $1,012. In conjunction with our forecast platinum prices, this results in a narrowing of the price differential between the two metals. Including 2011, this differential will have been stubbornly resilient at around the $1,000 mark for five years or so but is expected to contract to an average $645 by 2013. Despite a fairly bullish stance on platinum jewellery demand (notably in 2011 and 2012 when prices are especially high), these conditions are expected to continue over the forecast period, although the scale of the surplus is expected to moderate in 2012 and again in 2013. The principal reason for this persistent underlying surplus is the confluence of slender autocatalyst demand growth and increasing supply from mine production and recycling. Autocatalyst remains the largest element of fabrication demand but is heavily concentrated in diesel applications and in Europe’s light duty diesel market in particular (the world’s largest diesel market). Although improved in 2010, European light diesel production is far from achieving a full recovery and faces headwinds from Europe’s sovereign debt crisis together with the effects of widespread public spending cuts and tax increases across the region. Furthermore, platinum demand in light duty diesel is suffering continuing pressure from substitution (in favour of palladium) which is negating the beneficial effects of production growth and favourable emissions standards. As a result, the moderate demand growth we are forecasting for platinum in autocatalyst is instead entirely attributable to heavy duty applications, where the onroad sector is in recovery mode and off-road is newly emerging. Economic Assumptions** ###### **2.1 Introduction** GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case scenario, Scenario B and Scenario C. Under our Base Case projections we expect to see a slowdown in global GDP growth this year, partly as the effect of fiscal stimulus plans subside, before a gradual pick up in economic growth occurs over the final two years of our forecast due to improvements in the underlying world economy. We view this as the most likely scenario and since our March forecast the probability of our Base Case Scenario has remained unchanged at 50%. Our more bullish Scenario B, to which we assign a 30% probability, predicts inflation rising over the next three years, albeit modestly at first, and above all in the United States. Central to this scenario are the policies being followed by the US government and the Federal Reserve. These include a continuation of the very loose fiscal and monetary policy including further quantitative easing. Such policies are forecast to largely avert a renewed economic slowdown during 2011-13 but at the cost of rising inflation, with it reaching an annual average of 5.5% in 2013. Moreover, the US dollar weakens under this scenario. Under our bearish Scenario C, assigned a 20% probability, we expect government measures to have little impact on longer run economic growth as the global economy struggles to escape deflation. Consequently, global GDP growth slows appreciably in 2011 and remains sluggish over much of the remainder of the forecast, particularly in the developed world. The section below starts by describing the background to the current economic situation. We then discuss in more detail each of the three economic scenarios and, finall

y, comment on what impact each of these could have on gold prices between now and the end of 2013. ###### **2.2 Economic Backdrop** Since our last quarterly outlook, the world economy has been buffeted by a number of exogenous shocks including the ongoing ‘“Arab uprising” and the earthquake in Japan. The former has seen rising pressure on oil prices, while the latter has tempered global growth prospects. What remains unchanged is the feeling of generalised uncertainty concerning growth and inflationary prospects globally. As with the previous forecast, we expect to see a slowdown in world economic growth in 2011. In the developing world, where inflationary pressures have been growing, it is anticipated that monetary and fiscal authorities will adopt policies to moderate growth. Meanwhile, in the developed world this slower pace of economic growth is mainly a result of the unsustainability of government deficits, which have been crucial to the reflating of the global economy over the past eighteen months. An integral part of this is the absence of further fiscal stimulus or, in some European countries, outright fiscal austerity measures in an attempt to avert, or manage, sovereign debt crises. In fact, a look at government bond spreads between Eurozone countries indicates that the bloc’s sovereign debt crisis remains still acute. In addition, the austerity measures triggered by the crisis have clouded prospects for healthier GDP growth in Europe this year. Meanwhile, across the Atlantic the risk of a severe economic slowdown in the United States, where consumer spending is constrained by elevated debt levels and high unemployment, brought about a response from the authorities in the final third of 2010. As a result, in September the Federal Reserve indicated its willingness to make further asset purchases to support the recovery. Additionally, the extension of the entire ‘Bush’ tax cuts was unexpectedly agreed in December, as well as a further small fiscal stimulus. Consequently, although we anticipate a drop in the growth rate for US economy in 2011, it is expected to be more muted than was previously the case. |**~~Real GDP Growth Rates~~**

###### **2.3 Base Case Scenario** 

Our forecast for **global economic growth** in 2011 is largely unchanged since the March report.  After a major rebound in 2010, world GDP growth is set to slow down this year to 2.9%, up slightly from 2.8% in our previous forecast.  This is due to the indebted nature of both governments and consumers in much of the developed world.  In addition, a potential spike in oil and commodity prices, on the back of continued tensions in the Middle East and North Africa, could dampen confidence and weaken consumer spending. Meanwhile, further tightening of monetary policies in emerging markets to flight surging inflation will also slow down world GDP growth this year.  This is followed by marginally faster growth in 2012 and 2013 as the more traditional sources of growth, such as consumer spending and property market values, start to improve. The latter part of the forecast period will be aided by unemployment beginning to slowly recede, albeit from elevated levels. 

Following a pick-up in economic activity in late 2010, **US** GDP growth has slowed down, to 1.8% in the first quarter of this year, reflecting the underlying weak economy.  While economic growth could benefit from the Federal Reserve’s ongoing policies, room for further fiscal easing is becoming increasingly limited.  As a result, while a recovery in the labour market remains lacklustre, and with property prices showing little sign of improving, we expect economic growth to remain sluggish this year.  Furthermore, although monetary policy will remain extremely loose this year, increasing inflationary pressure and requests for higher yield on its treasury bonds from developing countries will eventually see the Federal Reserve tighten its policies in 2012.  This, combined with waning support for federal fiscal policies, will certainly restrict annual GDP growth to around 2% in the final two years of the forecast. 

Despite renewed concerns over sovereign debt, the recovery in **EU-27** economic growth (as a whole) has been gaining traction, although intra-European growth differentials are set to widen.  In part, these 











differences are due to the lingering impact of the crisis and the accelerating fiscal adjustments. ###### **7.2 Platinum Overview** Investment demand for platinum so far this year has remained fairly strong. To a large extent, this is due to heightened investor interest in the precious metals complex, itself a result of ongoing loose monetary policies in major countries, renewed European sovereign debt crisis and rising inflation fears. However, also of importance was many investors’ belief that platinum will play ‘catch-up’ this year following its underperformance of palladium in 2009 and 2010. Although the unexpected Japanese earthquake in early March did raise certain concerns regarding the outlook for global automobile production this year, the metal soon found support at the mid-$1,700s, suggesting that investor interest in the metal remains little changed. As we have discussed in Chapter 6 of this report, while the disaster will undoubtedly have an adverse impact on Japanese car production in the near term, its influence on the global market for the full year will be very limited. Looking at the rest of this year, in contrast to GFMS’ previous 3-year PGM forecast, we now expect World Investment for platinum to rise instead of fall in 2011. Underpinning this is our expectation for continued zero to negative real interest rates, massive budget deficits and, in time, a resumption of the US dollar’s decline.
